title: CPU cache structure (set-associative)
summary: A CPU cache is organized into sets, each containing ways (lines). Address decomposition: tag (high bits) | set index (middle bits) | block offset (low bits). On access: compute set index, check all ways in that set for a tag match. Hit: return data. Miss: fetch from next level. Replacement policies: LRU, pseudo-LRU, random, FIFO. Write policies: write-through (write to cache and memory) or write-back (write to cache only, dirty bit marks modified lines).

structure.meaning: Low bits: offset within the cache line. E.g., 6 bits for 64-byte lines.
Middle bits: which set. E.g., 6 bits for 64 sets.
High bits: identifies which memory block is in this line.
The unit of transfer between cache levels and memory.
Modified (dirty, exclusive), Exclusive (clean, exclusive), Shared (clean, may be in other caches), Invalid (not valid). Used for cache coherence in multi-core systems.
Write to cache only; mark line dirty. Write to memory only on eviction. Faster but requires dirty bit.
Write to cache and memory simultaneously. Simpler but slower.
Inclusive: L2 contains all L1 data. Exclusive: L2 and L1 are disjoint (more total capacity).

notes: L1 cache: small (32-64KB), fast (1-4 cycles), per-core.
L2 cache: medium (256KB-1MB), slower (4-12 cycles), per-core or shared.
L3 cache: large (4-64MB), slower (12-40 cycles), shared across cores.
Cache misses are the primary performance bottleneck in modern CPUs.
MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) is the standard cache coherence protocol.
